title: The Carpenter of San Gabriel
story:
Fifty-eight days after taking his first tentative steps beyond the Great Canopy, James woke to the scent of damp earth, woodsmoke, and bruised jacaranda blossoms. He lingered on the low stone wall at the village edge, letting the morning sounds wash over him.

He listened to the clatter of a tin kettle behind a cracked wooden shutter. He listened to the steady, rhythmic scrape of a straw broom clearing dried husks from an earthen stoop. He listened to the soft lowing of a lone goat tied beneath an avocado tree. In Oakhaven, the stone had been grand, towering, and measured to the ticking precision of brass gears; here in Aldea San Gabriel, the adobe walls leaned with age, flaking their lime wash to reveal dark sun-baked straw, and mountain ferns sprouted bravely between the cracked terracotta roof tiles. It was worn, but it was deeply, peacefully alive.

James hopped down from the wall and padded softly along the overgrown cobblestone lane. His brass canister knocked gently against his flank, the colorful threads woven by Mateo humming with familiar color in the highland daylight. The lane wound downward until it opened into a quiet, sleepy plaza bordered by overgrown squash vines and pepper trees. At the corner of the square sat an open-sided timber workshop, where pale pine shavings curled across the packed dirt floor like golden ribbons.

Beneath the workshop awning, an elderly man in a faded canvas apron stood beside a rustic workbench, smoothing a long plank with a hand plane. The rhythmic *shhh-shhh* of the iron blade against wood filled the cool air. James did not dart into the shadows. He simply paused at the edge of the awning and sat atop an upturned mossy stone, watching the carpenter work with quiet patience.

The man paused mid-stroke, resting the plane against the timber. He looked up, his weathered face creased with lines earned under decades of highland sun. He did not shout or raise a broom; he only studied the small, attentive traveler sitting beside his wood shavings. Reaching into a clean cloth laid out beside his chisel roll, the carpenter broke off a crisp piece of toasted yellow tortilla and set it gently atop the low stone wall dividing the lane from the yard, nodding once in silent welcome.

James reached out, took the warm corn tostada, and ate it slowly, the roasted flavor earthy and grounding. Just beyond the open workshop, through a tangled thicket of wild elderberry, James noticed an old, freestanding adobe shed. Its weathered wooden door hung slightly ajar on iron hinges, its cracked tile roof catching the first slant of golden morning sun.
location: Central Plaza of Aldea San Gabriel
